0.title: A Strange Word, a Glad Truth
0.essay:
Aseity is not a word you hear at the school gate or in the queue at the supermarket. Many Christians have never met it. Yet it names one of the gladdest truths in the Bible: God needs nothing. He does not need your help, your praise or your success. He does not even need the universe. And because he needs nothing, everything he gives you is pure gift.

What the word means

The word comes from two Latin words, a se, which mean “from himself”. Everything else that exists comes from something else. You came from your parents. Your bread came from wheat, rain and a baker’s early morning. God alone is from himself. He has life that nobody gave him, joy that nothing feeds and glory that no one can add to. Theologians speak of his self-existence, meaning that he depends on nothing for his being, and his self-sufficiency, meaning that he lacks nothing for his happiness.

Why it matters

Think of the difference between a present from a friend who simply loves you and a present from someone who wants something back. Our hearts are always tempted to treat God like the second kind of giver, and ourselves as people who must keep him supplied. Aseity ends that. A God who needed us would love us with strings attached. A God who needs nothing can only love us freely. He cannot be bribed or worn out. He did not make you because he was lonely, and he did not save you because heaven was short-staffed.

The study The Attributes of God sets aseity beside God’s eternity and unchangeableness in its chapter God in Himself: Eternal, Independent, Unchanging, and the dictionary entry Aseity gives a short definition. This study stays with this one truth a little longer, and asks what it does to the heart.

The chapters

I AM WHO I AM; Love Before the World; Grace That Cannot Be a Transaction; The Self-Sufficient One Made Needy; Security for Needy People; and Living Before the God Who Needs Nothing.

For reflection

Do you ever feel, deep down, that God needs you to keep him happy, or to keep his work going? What would change if you knew that every good thing he gives you is a gift, with nothing owed?

1.title: I AM WHO I AM
1.essay:
An eighty-year-old shepherd sees a thornbush on fire in the desert. That is nothing unusual: dry scrub catches easily and is ash in minutes. What makes Moses stop is that this fire goes on burning, and the bush is not used up.

The fire that needs no fuel

“He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2). Every fire we know is hungry. It lives by eating, and when the wood is gone, so is the fire. Moses could not make sense of it: “I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned” (Exodus 3:3).

Before God told Moses his name, he showed him a picture of it. Here was a fire that fed on nothing. And notice the second wonder: the bush was not destroyed. The God who needs nothing does not devour what he comes near to. He can dwell in a humble desert shrub and leave it whole. He does not draw his life from his creatures. He gives it.

A name that is a sentence

Moses asked what he should tell Israel when they wanted to know God’s name. God answered, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). The gods of the nations around were usually named for what they did or ruled: a storm, a river, a harvest. This name is not about a job. It is about being itself. The name the LORD, which follows in the next verse, is closely linked to that same Hebrew verb “to be”.

Only God can simply say, “I AM.” He is not becoming anything, not growing into anything and not waiting for anything. Moses later sang of it: “Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2).

Life in himself

Jesus said, “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). Notice that it is said of the Son as well. The word “granted” does not mean the Son was once without life and later received it, as a creature does. It describes the eternal relation of the Son to the Father: the Son is eternally begotten, sharing the one undivided life of God. That is why John can say of the Word, “In him was life” (John 1:4). He did not borrow it. It is his.

If I were hungry

Israel sometimes treated their sacrifices as if they were feeding God. In Psalm 50 God answers with holy humour. “I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills” (Psalm 50:9–10). Then the punchline: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (Psalm 50:12).

Paul said the same thing to the people of Athens, in a city crowded with shrines and altars. God is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25). The traffic runs one way. We do not keep God going. He keeps us going, breath by breath.

What aseity is not

Some imagine that a God who needs nothing must be distant and cool. The opposite is true. The God of the burning bush said, in the same conversation, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people” (Exodus 3:7). He came down to rescue them. Needing nothing does not make him uncaring. It makes his care free.

One related teaching needs care. The old confessions describe God as being without body, parts or passions, which is called impassibility. Some modern theologians reject this, fearing it makes God a cold statue, and argue that a God who truly loves must be moved and even suffer in his divine nature, just as we are. Others hold the historic teaching, noting that “passions” in the old sense meant feelings that come over a person from outside, change them and sometimes overwhelm them.

This commentary’s view: God’s love, joy, compassion and anger are real and perfect, but they are not moods forced on him by events. He is never at the mercy of what we do. His love is not squeezed out of him by our misery; it is his free and settled purpose, which is exactly why it can be trusted. And God the Son, having taken a real human nature, truly wept, suffered and died in that nature, as a later chapter shows. Aseity and impassibility belong together. A God who needed something could be wounded at the core by its loss and might, in the end, give up. The God who needs nothing loves from fullness, and fullness does not run dry.

An example

A woman in her fifties runs the church’s food bank, the Sunday school rota and the prayer chain. Without ever saying so, she feels God would struggle without her. One week, worn out, she reads Psalm 50 and laughs out loud at verse 12. She is not offended but relieved, and that night she sleeps well for the first time in months.

For reflection

What does the bush that was not consumed tell you about God? Why is it good news that God says, “If I were hungry, I would not tell you” (Psalm 50:12)? In what ways do you act as if God depends on you? How does the steadiness of God’s love comfort you in a changing week?

2.title: Love Before the World
2.essay:
Before there was a sun, a star or a single angel, there was love. Not a lonely God waiting for company, but Father, Son and Holy Spirit living in perfect delight. Everything God has made, and everything he has done to save us, flows out of that love. None of it was needed to fill a gap.

What was God doing before the world?

Augustine records a joking answer someone gave, that God was preparing hell for people who ask such questions, and says he would rather not answer that way. Jesus gives us the real answer, and it is beautiful. On the night before he died he prayed, “And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). A few verses later he spoke of the glory the Father had given him “because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24).

Before anything was made, the Father was loving the Son, and the Son was rejoicing in the Father, in the Holy Spirit. There was glory, love and joy, complete and unending. The study The Trinity explains the three persons and the one God more fully. Here we notice one thing: God was never lonely.

Not a remedy for loneliness

It is common to imagine that God made people because he wanted someone to love, as if he were incomplete without us. It sounds kind, but it quietly makes God needy and us his medicine. If that were true, we would always have to keep him happy, and our failures might break his heart beyond repair.

The Bible says something better. “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and he has always been love, because the Father has always loved the Son. Love did not begin when we arrived. We were not brought in to rescue God from an empty house. We were invited into a house already full of joy.

Overflow and delight

So why did God create at all? Not from need, but from fullness. Think of a spring high in the hills that simply cannot help overflowing. “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light” (Psalm 36:9). Jonathan Edwards, the eighteenth-century pastor, argued that God did not make the world to gain a glory he lacked, but to share the fullness he already had, as a fountain pours out its water.

That is why the creation story rings with delight. “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). God enjoys what he makes, the way an artist enjoys a finished painting, not the way a hungry man enjoys a meal.

Redemption is overflow too. The Father did not send the Son because heaven had run short of worshippers. He sent him because love that is full wants to give itself away.

His glory is his joy shared

Some people stumble when the Bible says God does everything for his own glory. Is that not vain? It would be, for a creature. But think it through. If God is the greatest good there is, then the most loving thing he can do is give us himself. When God seeks his glory, he is not grabbing something from us. He is opening his life to us.

Listen to Jesus. He wants his people “to see my glory” (John 17:24). He prays “that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17:26). He says, “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11). The glory of God and the joy of his people are not rivals. His glory is his joy, shared.

Wanted, not needed

Here is what this does to the heart. Someone who needs you may love you, but there is always a question: would they still want me if I were no longer useful? God’s love has no such question in it. Moses told Israel, “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The reason God loves you is not in you. It is in him.

That means you are not needed, and you are utterly wanted. And because his love never depended on your usefulness, it will not cool when your usefulness fades.

An example

A man in his forties was the eldest child in a struggling family. From the age of ten he held things together. He became the person everyone relied on, at home, at work and at church. He assumed God valued him the same way. Reading John 17 one morning, he stops at the words “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24) and realises that the Father’s love for the Son was full long before anyone needed anything. He is invited into that love, not employed by it.

For reflection

What difference does it make that God was never lonely? Why might it be dangerous to think God created us because he needed us? How does Jesus’ prayer in John 17 describe what God wants to share with you? Where do you most need to hear that you are wanted, not merely needed?

3.title: Grace That Cannot Be a Transaction
3.essay:
Most religion, and most of our hearts, runs on a simple deal. I give to God, and God gives back. I am good, so God owes me a good life. Aseity breaks that deal into pieces, and the breaking is some of the best news you will ever hear.

Who has given first?

Paul spends eleven chapters of Romans showing that salvation is all of grace. Then he bursts into praise. “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). He asks, “Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35). Then he answers his own question: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

Paul is echoing God’s words to Job: “Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine” (Job 41:11). No one has ever got in first with God. No one has handed him something he did not already own, so no one has ever put him in debt.

Of your own have we given

King David once led Israel in an enormous offering for the temple, gold and silver and precious stones given gladly by the people. Yet David’s prayer is full of humility: “For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

It is like a small child who borrows money from her father to buy him a birthday present. The father is truly delighted, but nobody imagines he has been made richer. Paul asks the same thing of us: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Our gifts to God are real, and he loves them. But they are always his gifts first.

Unworthy servants

Jesus put it bluntly. “So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty’” (Luke 17:10). This does not mean God sneers at our service. Jesus also promised that his faithful servants will hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). But even that reward is grace. Augustine said that when God crowns our good works, he is crowning his own gifts.

So you cannot put God in your debt. And here is the freedom: you never need to try.

The elder brother

Jesus told a story about two sons. The younger ran off and wasted everything. The elder stayed at home and worked hard. When the younger came back and his father threw a party, the elder brother was furious. He said, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (Luke 15:29).

He talks like an employee, not a son. He has been keeping accounts. His obedience was a way of getting something out of his father. Timothy Keller has shown how this parable exposes two ways of running from God: one by breaking the rules, the other by keeping them in order to have a claim on him.

The father’s answer is tender: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). You do not have to earn what you already have. Paul makes the same contrast: “Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due” (Romans 4:4). A God who needs nothing cannot pay wages. He can only give.

Worship and service as receiving

So what is worship, if it adds nothing to God? It is opening our hands. In Psalm 50, straight after saying he is not hungry, God tells his people what he wants: “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving” (Psalm 50:14), and “call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 50:15). God delivers, we are glad, and that gladness honours him. The God who needs nothing is glorified most when we come to him as needy people and go away filled.

Service is the same: not keeping God supplied, but overflow from what we have been given.

The end of the fear of failing God

Many Christians live with a low hum of dread: have I let God down? Our sins are real, and they grieve him. But you cannot bankrupt someone whose riches never came from you. Your worst week does not empty his grace or shrink his joy. And grace does not make sin unimportant. When Paul asks whether we should go on sinning so that grace may abound, he answers, “By no means!” (Romans 6:2). Free people obey out of gratitude, not to keep up the payments. The study The Grace of God takes this further in its chapter Grace Against Legalism and Licence.

An example

A man has been a deacon for thirty years: never missing a meeting, always setting out the chairs. When a former addict is baptised and the whole church celebrates, he feels a cold resentment he cannot explain. Talking with his pastor, he sees the elder brother in himself, keeping score. Slowly, he begins to set out the chairs for joy, not for credit, and to rejoice when others are welcomed.

For reflection

Where do you notice yourself “keeping accounts” with God? How does 1 Chronicles 29:14 change the way you think about giving? Which brother in Luke 15 are you more like? What would it mean for you to stop trying to put God in your debt?

4.title: The Self-Sufficient One Made Needy
4.essay:
Here is the wonder at the centre of the Christian faith. The God who needs nothing became a man who needed everything: milk from his mother’s breast, sleep, bread, water, a borrowed boat, and at the last a borrowed grave.

The Word became flesh

John begins his Gospel with the eternal Word who “was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and in whom was life. Then comes one of the most astonishing sentences ever written: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Paul describes the same step downward. Christ, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7).

He did not stop being God. He emptied himself by taking, not by losing: he added a real human nature to his divine nature, and became one person who is both. John Calvin marvelled that the Son came down from heaven without leaving heaven, so that the baby in Mary’s arms was still upholding the universe. Even as an infant he was the one who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

Hungry, tired and thirsty

The Gospels do not hide how needy he became. After forty days in the wilderness, “he was hungry” (Matthew 4:2). In a storm he was “in the stern, asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38), worn out.

Then there is the scene at the well in Samaria. “Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well” (John 4:6). A woman came to draw water, and the Lord of life said to her, “Give me a drink” (John 4:7). The one who made every spring on earth asked a stranger for a cup of water. And in the same conversation he offered her “living water” (John 4:10). He received in order to give. His humble asking opened the way for her to receive what she most needed.

I thirst

On the cross, near the end, he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). The fountain of life was dry. Why? Because he was taking our place, entering our lack, our curse and our death, so that we could share his fullness. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Because the Son is one person, the Bible can even say that they “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). God the Son suffered, truly and terribly, in the human nature he had taken. That is why we have a high priest who is able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

Life laid down, not taken

Here aseity makes the cross even more astonishing. Every other person who has ever died had their life taken from them. Jesus said, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18).

Only someone with life in himself could say that. He was not a victim of need. He did not die because he ran out of strength or because events overpowered him. He gave himself, freely, out of fullness. The cross was not God being drained against his will. It was God giving, as he always gives, from a love that cannot be exhausted. Paul could say, with wonder, that he “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Life that death could not hold

Death works by draining. It starves the body of breath and blood until nothing is left. But on Good Friday death met someone who did not draw his life from anything outside himself. Peter preached, “God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

Think again of the burning bush. The fire entered the thornbush and was not put out, and the thornbush was not destroyed. At Calvary the Son entered death itself, the thorny ground of the curse, and death could not consume him. Instead, on the third day, life came blazing out. And now he offers that endless life to everyone who comes to him: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35).

An example

A proud, capable man in his sixties has a stroke. For months he has to be fed, washed and helped to dress. He hates it. He feels useless and ashamed. A friend reads him John 4 and points out that the Son of God asked for a drink. The man is silent for a while. Then he says, “So he knows what this is like.” From that day he finds it a little easier to say thank you.

For reflection

What strikes you most about the Lord of life asking for a drink? How does it change the cross to know that no one took Jesus’ life from him? Why could death not hold him? Where do you find it hard to receive help from others, and how might Jesus’ example help you?

5.title: Security for Needy People
5.essay:
We are needy people. We need food and sleep, friends and forgiveness, help in the morning and rest at night. That is not a design fault. Creatures are made to depend. The only question is what, or whom, we depend on.

The God who never runs out

Isaiah wrote to people who felt forgotten. They said, “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God” (Isaiah 40:27). Isaiah answers by pointing them to who God is: “The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable” (Isaiah 40:28).

Then he turns to us. “He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted; but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:29–31). The strongest people run out. God never does. And because he never runs out, he can give and give without becoming any less.

The keeper who never sleeps

“He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:3–4). Every human carer has limits: parents fall asleep, nurses go off shift. But the one who keeps you is never off duty.

And that means you can sleep. You are not holding the world together through the night. The study Busy, Tired & Restless explores sleep and rest as gifts in its chapter Dust, Sleep and the Seventh Day.

Asking a God who needs nothing

Jesus said, “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8). Then why pray? Not to inform God, as if he were short of news, nor to wear down a reluctant giver. We pray because he delights to be asked. A good father knows what his child needs, yet he loves to hear the child ask, because asking is trust, and trust is the heart of the relationship. “How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11).

God has also chosen to give many things through our asking. Our prayers do not add to his power, but in his kindness he has made them part of how his purposes come about. That gives prayer real dignity.

Paul promised the Philippians, “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). Notice: “according to” his riches, not merely “out of” them. A billionaire who gives you ten pounds gives out of his riches. God gives in proportion to his riches, and they never shrink.

Not the world’s saviour

Some of the most faithful Christians burn out because, without ever saying it, they believe God’s work depends on them. If they stop, it will collapse. Paul punctures that gently. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

This is humbling, and it is a huge relief. You are not the Messiah. The gospel will go on if you take a holiday. Jesus himself said to his weary disciples, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31).

The humility and dignity of dependence

Here is the surprising thing. The God who does not need us still chooses to use us. A father painting a fence does not need his four-year-old’s help. It would be quicker without her. But he puts a small brush in her hand because he loves to work alongside her. Our work for God is like that. It is not required to keep him going. It is invited because he loves us. That is both humbling and full of dignity.

So depending on God is not humiliating. It is what we were made for. Jesus said, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and he said it as a vine speaks to its branches, not as a master to his slaves.

A word of care. Anxiety and exhaustion are sometimes more than spiritual struggles. If worry or low mood has taken hold for weeks, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself, please speak to a doctor and to someone you trust, and in an emergency contact emergency services or a crisis line straight away. Taking medicine or seeing a counsellor is no failure of faith. God often supplies our needs through doctors and friends.

An example

A woman leads a small Christian charity for refugees. For six years she has not taken a proper holiday, sure that families would be let down if she did. After a collapse at work, her doctor signs her off for two months. Slowly she sees that the work carried on, held by others and by God. When she returns, she keeps a weekly day off, and she prays more and frets less.

For reflection

Where are you most aware of your neediness at the moment? How does Isaiah 40:28–31 speak to that? Why pray if your Father already knows what you need? Is there any part of God’s work that you have quietly come to believe depends on you?

6.title: Living Before the God Who Needs Nothing
6.essay:
How do you live, day by day, before a God who needs nothing and gives everything? Not by trying to impress him, and not by trying to keep him supplied. You live by receiving, and then by giving freely what you have received.

Worship

In John’s vision of heaven, the twenty-four elders “cast their crowns before the throne” (Revelation 4:10). Every crown was his gift first. And they sing, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created” (Revelation 4:11).

Worship is not flattering a needy god to keep him in a good mood. It is the joy of creatures who see who God is and cannot help saying so. We do not make God glorious. We see that he is, and it fills us with delight.

Contentment

Paul wrote from prison, “I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content” (Philippians 4:11). He had found that Christ was enough. If you have God, you have the one who lacks nothing. “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26). It is resting our needs on someone who never runs out.

Generosity without anxiety

Fear of running short is one of the great enemies of generosity. But your Father owns the cattle on a thousand hills. “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace abound to you” (2 Corinthians 9:7–8). We can give without fear, because our supply comes from a fountain that does not fail. And we can give without strings, because we were given everything without strings. “You received without paying; give without pay” (Matthew 10:8).

Serving without fear

Many of us serve with a nervous eye on the verdict: will they think well of me? Will God be disappointed? But the one whose verdict matters has already loved you in Christ, and he does not need your service to be complete. So you can serve freely. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

There is deep joy here. You do not have to be needed by anyone to know you are worth something. Your worth was settled when God set his love on you. The study The Fear of Man explores this freedom from living for other people’s approval.

Daily habits

Truths like this grow in us through small, repeated habits.

Morning remembrance. Before reaching for your phone, remember that you woke because God gave you breath. “I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me” (Psalm 3:5). A sentence is enough: “Lord, I depend on you for everything today, and you will not run out.”

Thanksgiving. At the end of the day, name three things you received. It trains the heart to see life as gift rather than wages. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

The Lord’s Day as rest. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that Sunday is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law with rules about work. Others, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, and no one should bind another’s conscience here. Either way, a day of rest preaches a sermon: the world goes on when you stop, because God holds it, not you.

When God is all in all

The Bible ends where it began, with God’s fullness. Paul writes that at the end, when Christ has defeated every enemy, “the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). This does not mean the Son is less than the Father. It belongs to his work as our Mediator: the Son, having finished the work of salvation he freely took on, hands the rescued kingdom to the Father.

And then God will be all in all. Not that we disappear into him, but that everything will be filled with him. The needy will be needy no more, not because we stop depending on God, but because we will depend on him perfectly and gladly for ever. “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). The fire that needs no fuel will warm a whole new creation, and nothing in it will be consumed.

An example

A retired couple start each day with a cup of tea and a short prayer: “Thank you for breath, and for one another. We need you today.” Over the years they notice that they worry less about money, give more freely and argue less about who does what in church. They have simply learned, morning by morning, that God is enough.

For reflection

How does knowing that God needs nothing change the way you worship? Where do you need to give or serve more freely, without fear? Which of the daily habits could you begin this week? What do you most look forward to in the day when God will be all in all?
